blocks.text: The d-orbitals have a characteristic cloverleaf shape, generally resembling four lobes or two dumbbells in a plane, with five distinct orbitals dxy, dxz, dyz, dx²−y², and dz². In an isolated atom, all five d orbitals have the same energy (degenerate), but their different shapes lead to different energies in complex ions (non-degenerate). Their spatial (in space) arrangements and energy levels decide the bonding, colour, and magnetic properties of transition metals. When ligands approach the metal ion to form an octahedral or a tetrahedral complex, they create an electric field that causes the five d orbitals to split into two groups with different energies, making them non-degenerate. The energy difference is related to the extent of splitting between the two sets of orbitals and is represented by Δ.

In octahedral complexes (with six ligands), like [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺, the five d orbitals split into two sets; three lower-energy orbitals including, dxy, dxz, dyz and two higher-energy orbitals; dx²−y², dz² (Figure 18.4).

blocks.alt: Energy diagram with an upward Energy axis. Degenerate Orbitals: five equal boxes dxy, dyz, dzx, dx2-y2, dz2 with one electron. Ligands interaction: the five boxes raised. They then split: dx2-y2 and dz2 above, dxy, dyz and dzx below holding the electron, separated by Delta E. Light is absorbed and, after Excitation, the electron is in the upper set.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.4: Splitting of d orbitals in octahedral fields (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.4).

blocks.text: In tetrahedral complexes (with four ligands), like [CuCl₄]²⁻, the splitting is inverted with three higher-energy orbitals dxy, dxz, dyz and two lower-energy orbitals dx²−y², dz². The magnitude of splitting in tetrahedral complexes is smaller than that in octahedral complexes (Figure .18.5).

blocks.alt: Energy diagram for nine d electrons. Degenerate orbitals: five equal boxes, four with paired electrons and one with a single electron. Ligands interaction: the boxes raised. Split: dxy, dyz, dzx above (paired, paired, single) and dx2-y2, dz2 below (both paired), separated by Delta E. Light is absorbed and, after Excitation, the upper set is full and the lower set has one single electron.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.5: Splitting of d orbitals in tetrahedral fields (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.5).
